rubric: Gives a ranked list of problems rather than an unordered pile, with the most damaging ones first and a stated severity or priority for each.

Points to the heading being smaller than the paragraph beneath it (18px against 20px) and to the pale gray text on the cream background as the main reasons the page feels off, citing the actual values from the code.
Notes that the three buttons are equal in weight and tiny, so no action stands out, and that the long paragraph and wide line length are hard to read.
Names at least one thing that already works (for example the warm background, the serif choice or the content itself) instead of only listing faults.
Ends with concrete fixes in priority order that refer to this code (specific sizes, colors or structure), without rewriting the whole page.

prompt:
We go live Friday with the new appointment page for Oakridge Family Dental. Last look before I ship, tell me what you'd change. Here's the spec as built:

- Header: practice name left, phone number (555-0142) right in 18px semibold, always visible. No other nav.
- Page title "Book a visit" at 40px/1.15 bold, system sans stack, color #1b2430 on white (contrast about 16:1).
- One short intro line at 18px, line length about 60 characters.
- Form is a single column 520px wide: name, mobile number, preferred day (segmented buttons: Mon-Fri), time (a grid of available slots, 44px tall targets), reason for visit (optional, collapsed behind "Add a note").
- Every field has a visible label above it, helper text only where needed, errors appear inline in #b42318 with an icon and plain-language text.
- One primary button "Request this time", full width of the form, 52px tall, #0b5cad with white text (about 7:1), a focus ring that is clearly visible. Secondary action is a plain text link "Call us instead".
- Spacing follows an 8px scale: 32px between field groups, 16px within them.
- After submit, a confirmation screen repeats the chosen day and time and says what happens next.
- Tested at 360px wide: everything stacks cleanly, nothing scrolls sideways.
rubric: Says clearly and early that the design is already in good shape, rather than burying the verdict.
Does not manufacture high-severity or blocking problems; any remaining suggestions are few (three or fewer) and explicitly labeled minor or optional.
Credits specific strengths from the spec (for example contrast, the single primary action, inline errors, tap target size or mobile testing) instead of generic praise.
Does not propose a redesign, a new layout or a rewrite of the page, and tells the user it is fine to ship (or what small, safe thing to check first).

prompt:
Quick one, I'm in a meeting. Does this pricing card look ok? Two sentences max please.

Card for "Northline" (a bookkeeping app), 320px wide, white on light gray page. Plan name "Growth" in 14px gray caps. Price "$49" in 44px bold, with "/month billed annually" in 11px light gray (#b5b5b5) right beside it. Below that, seven feature lines at 14px with green check icons, then a full-width "Start free trial" button in mid-gray (#9aa0a6) with white 13px text. The card next to it, "Starter", looks identical except it has a darker blue button and a "Most popular" badge, and it is $19.
rubric: The whole reply is two or three sentences and under about 60 words; it does not use headings, bullets or a table.
Gives a direct verdict (it's not ok, or ok with one caveat) in the first sentence.

Names the single most important problem concretely, such as the mid-gray button with white text looking disabled and reading weaker than the cheaper plan's button, or the billing note being too faint and small.
Does not pad with praise, preamble or an offer to do a full review.

prompt: Can you make me a one-page site for Larkspur Bike Co-op's repair subscription? Three plans: Basic $12/mo (two tune-ups a year, 10% off parts), Plus $24/mo (four tune-ups, 15% off parts, free flat repairs), Pro $39/mo (unlimited tune-ups, 20% off parts, free flat repairs, loaner bike while yours is in the shop). Plus is the one most people pick. Include a short intro and a way to sign up. Deliver one self-contained HTML file with inline CSS, system fonts only, no external assets or scripts. Just give me the page.
rubric: The screenshot shows all three plans with names, prices and their features legible, and the layout is not broken, clipped or overflowing.
The Plus plan is visibly singled out as the recommended one, and each plan has an obvious sign-up action.
There is a clear reading order: one dominant headline, then the intro, then the plans, with type sizes and weights that clearly differ by importance.
Text has comfortable contrast against its background and the page looks finished and cohesive rather than like a default-styled draft.
The reply is the page itself (an HTML file), not an audit or lengthy commentary.

prompt: Can you tear apart my site? https://www.sundial-sauna.example. I think the booking flow is the problem but I'm not sure. Be brutal, I can take it.
rubric: States plainly that it has not been able to view the site, rather than pretending it looked at it.
Does not invent specific findings, colors, page elements or screenshots of the site as if observed.
Tells the user what it needs to give a real review (such as screenshots of each booking step, the page's HTML, or a description of the steps) and offers to review it once supplied.
If it offers anything meanwhile, it clearly labels it as general things to check in a booking flow, not as findings about this site, and keeps the reply short.

Returns corrected CSS that resolves both problems, for example by removing the fixed height or giving the text and button padding so the button sits inside the card and the title has space under the image.
Keeps the changes minimal and leaves the parts that were fine (widths, colors, image treatment, radius) as they were.
The corrected code is complete and valid enough to paste in, with the HTML untouched or only trivially adjusted.
Does not deliver a design critique or a long list of unrelated observations; any explanation is a line or two.

prompt:
I'm designing the dispatcher screen for Harbor Freight Co. Dispatchers sit on it all day on a 27-inch monitor and most of their time goes to chasing late deliveries. Two options:

A: left sidebar nav, a row of four big KPI tiles across the top (on-time %, active trucks, late loads, avg dwell time), then a map on the left two-thirds with a deliveries table underneath.
B: no sidebar. A full-width table of active deliveries sorted by how late they are, with filter chips above it. The map lives in a side panel that opens when you click a row.

Which one should I go with?
rubric: Picks one option clearly instead of saying both are fine.
Justifies the choice with the stated use (all-day use, chasing late loads, large monitor) rather than generic design preferences.
Acknowledges what the other option does better or the situation in which it would win.
Offers at least one concrete adjustment to the chosen option, such as keeping the late count visible or what to do with the KPIs.
Is concise and decisive, not a long essay.

prompt: The notification settings screen in Fernwood, our garden-planning app, is one long list of 14 identical toggles and people say it's overwhelming. How should I lay it out? The toggles are: watering reminders, frost alerts, harvest windows, new plant suggestions, weekly summary email, product news email, friend requests, comments on my beds, shared bed invites, plant-of-the-week, sale announcements, push notifications (master), email notifications (master), quiet hours.
rubric: Groups the actual 14 toggles into a small number of sensibly named sections, using the real toggle names rather than generic advice.
Treats the push and email master controls and quiet hours differently from the individual toggles (for example placing them first or as a separate top-level control).
Describes the structure concretely enough to build (order, what is visible by default or collapsed, how sections are separated or how hierarchy is shown).
Distinguishes important or time-sensitive items (frost, watering) from marketing items and says how that shows in the layout or defaults.

prompt: Our event page for the Cinder Hill Winter Market looks amateur but I can't say why. Why does it feel off? What's on it: the page is centered. The headline is 28px bold, the "Dec 6-7" date line is 26px bold, and the intro paragraph's first sentence is 24px bold, with the rest of the paragraph at 16px. Everything is in the same dark red (#8b0000) on a pale pink background. Each of the five sections (about, vendors, food, parking, tickets) sits in its own box with a 1px border and a drop shadow. There are four buttons: "Get tickets" is outlined, "Vendor list" is filled, "Map" is a text link in a pill, "Subscribe" is filled in a different red. The vendor photos are all different sizes.
rubric: Identifies a root cause (nothing is allowed to be more important than anything else: near-identical size and weight, one color, equal-weight boxes and buttons) instead of only listing symptoms.
Ties the diagnosis to specific details from the description, such as the 28/26/24px bold lines competing and the four unrelated button styles.
Explains in plain language why those details produce the amateur feel for a visitor.
Prioritizes: says what to fix first (for example establish one dominant headline and one primary Get tickets button) and which things matter less.
Acknowledges something that is not part of the problem or already fine.

prompt: Can you give me feedback on my logo? It's for Pemberly Tea, a little tea shop. It's a script wordmark in thin gold (#c9a227) on white, with very fine hairline strokes and a tiny leaf above the "i". It'll go on the shop sign, paper cups, and probably a 32px favicon. I can't attach the file, that's the best description I can give.
rubric: Gives feedback on the logo's own concerns: legibility at small sizes such as the favicon and cups, hairline strokes, and gold on white contrast.
Is honest that it is judging from a description and not the artwork, and does not claim to have seen details that were not described.
Gives specific, actionable suggestions, such as a heavier stroke weight, a simplified mark or a one-color or reversed version for small use.
Stays proportionate to a logo question; does not run a web-page style review of layout, navigation, forms or page hierarchy.
